summary: Updates the recommendation on TLS for protecting email between a user's mail program and a submission or access server, so that TLS 1.1 is no longer recommended. It updates RFC 8314.

eli5.summary: Email programs should stop using an outdated version of the lock that protects messages and use newer ones.

questions: which tls version for imap and smtp submission
what is the minimum tls version for email
why was tls 1.1 deprecated for email
which tls version should mail clients require
subtitle: Email clients and servers should now require TLS 1.2 or later, not TLS 1.1, for submission and access.

tldr.problem: RFC 8314 set TLS 1.1 as the minimum recommended version for email submission and access, but TLS 1.1 was later deprecated in RFC 8996.
tldr.mechanism: This document edits specific passages of RFC 8314 so that every 'TLS 1.1 or greater' requirement becomes 'TLS 1.2 or greater'.
tldr.outcome: TLS 1.2 is the new minimum for mail user agents and mail service providers. The document updates RFC 8314 and has no IANA actions.

today: RFC 8997 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2021 and it updates RFC 8314. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why RFC 8314 Needs Updating
sections.content:
RFC 8314 defines the minimum recommended version of TLS for protecting email between a Mail User Agent (MUA) and a mail submission or mail access server as version 1.1. Because TLS 1.1 has since been deprecated in RFC 8996, that recommendation is no longer valid.

This document therefore updates RFC 8314 so that the minimum version for TLS is TLS 1.2. It does nothing else: it introduces no new protocol and no new mechanism.
sections.eli5: An older rule said a certain old lock was good enough for email. That lock was later retired, so the rule has to be changed to name a newer lock.

sections.title: The Edits to RFC 8314
sections.content:
The document is written as a list of OLD and NEW text blocks, all in Section 4.1 of RFC 8314 (and the MUA requirements). In each block, the version number 1.1 is replaced by 1.2.

  • The section heading changes from 'TLS Versions Less Than 1.1' to 'TLS Versions Less Than 1.2'.
  • The recommendation that new users be required to use TLS version 1.1 or greater becomes 1.2 or greater.
  • The default minimum confidentiality level for new accounts SHOULD require negotiation of TLS version 1.2 or greater, and it MUST still require successful validation of the server's certificate.
sections.eli5: It is a find-and-replace job. Everywhere the old rule said 'version 1.1', the new rule says 'version 1.2'.

sections.title: What Providers Should Do
sections.content:
Mail service providers (MSPs) that still support SSL 2.x, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 SHOULD move their users to TLS 1.2 or later as soon as practicable, and stop supporting the earlier versions. The old text stopped at TLS 1.0; the new text adds TLS 1.1 to the list to be dropped.

One way to enforce this is for the server to refuse a ClientHello message from any client sending a ClientHello.version field that corresponds to any version of SSL or TLS earlier than TLS 1.2. New users SHOULD be required to use TLS 1.2 or greater from the start, although an MSP may still make exceptions for legacy systems that support only earlier versions of TLS or only cleartext.
sections.eli5: Mail providers should switch their customers to the newer lock and stop accepting the old ones. They can turn away anyone who shows up with an old lock, though they may make exceptions for very old devices.

sections.title: What Mail Programs Must Do
sections.content:
MUAs MUST implement TLS 1.2 or later, and the document now gives TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) as an example of a later version. Earlier TLS and SSL versions MAY also be supported, as long as the MUA requires at least TLS 1.2 when accessing accounts that are configured to impose minimum confidentiality requirements.

If an MUA gives the user an indication of confidentiality, it MUST NOT claim confidentiality for any connection that does not at least use TLS 1.2 with certificate verification and also meet the minimum requirements of that account.
sections.eli5: A mail app must know how to use the newer lock. It may not show the 'safe' sign unless the newer lock is on and the app has checked who it is talking to.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. The purpose of the document is to record updated recommendations for using TLS with email services, and those recommendations are based on RFC 8996. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The reason for the change is simply that the older lock was officially retired. Nothing new needs to be registered anywhere.
